The [Skill collection](skill-collection.qmd) lists what the sessions built.
This page is how to build the next one yourself. It takes no code: a skill is
a plain-English file, and Claude writes most of it for you. Terms are defined
in the [Thesaurus](thesaurus.qmd).

Each step ends with a line to tick. Ticks are saved in your browser only.

## The lifecycle

### 1. Notice the pattern

A task deserves a skill when you recognise any of these:

- you have typed roughly the same request more than twice;
- you walk Claude through the same steps in the same order every time;
- you keep supplying the same background ("our template", "ten pages at most").

One-off tasks do not need one. Neither does anything you have not yet done by
hand: you cannot write down a procedure you have not followed.

::: {#skill-step-1 .checklist .selfcheck}
- [ ] I have a task in mind that I have explained to Claude at least three times
:::

### 2. Do it by hand once more

Run the task in an ordinary conversation, in the folder where the files live,
and pay attention to yourself. What did you have to correct? What did Claude
get wrong on the first try? What did you paste in? Those corrections are the
skill; everything else Claude would have done anyway.

::: {#skill-step-2 .checklist .selfcheck}
- [ ] I have done the task once in conversation and I know what I corrected
:::

### 3. Have Claude write it

Stay in the same conversation, so the corrections are still in context, and
ask:

```text
Turn what we just did into a skill called /my-task in this project's
.claude/skills/ folder. Write the procedure as numbered steps in plain English.
Include every correction I made as an explicit instruction. Before it writes
the final file, the skill must show me its plan and wait for my go-ahead.
```

What comes back is a folder with one file, `.claude/skills/my-task/SKILL.md`.
Open it and read it; it should look like this:

```markdown
---
name: my-task
description: "One sentence: what it does and when to use it."
---

# /my-task

## Trigger
User runs: `/my-task [optional: file or folder]`
If no input is given, ask which one to use.

## Steps
1. Read the defaults in `CLAUDE.md`.
2. Read the input and ...
3. Show the proposed plan and wait for confirmation.
4. Write the result to `output/`.

## If something goes wrong
- No input found: say so and stop.
- A file cannot be read: list it, continue with the rest.

## Report back
Print what was written and where.
```

The `name` must match the folder name. The `description` is what Claude reads
to decide when the skill applies, so make it specific. Whatever you type after
the command is available to the skill as `$ARGUMENTS`.

::: {#skill-step-3 .checklist .selfcheck}
- [ ] `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` exists and I have read it
:::

### 4. Test it in a fresh session

The conversation that wrote the skill already knows what you want, so it is the
wrong place to test it. Start a new session, type `/`, check the skill is
listed, and run it on a real input. Judge the output yourself. Typical first
results and their fixes:

| What you see | What to add to the skill |
|---|---|
| Too long, too chatty | A length limit and an exact output format |
| It guessed something you would have told it | The missing instruction, or a line in `CLAUDE.md` |
| Wrong structure | A template of the output, headings included |
| It fell over on an odd input | A line under "If something goes wrong" |

Fix by asking, not by editing: tell Claude what went wrong and have it update
the file.

::: {#skill-step-4 .checklist .selfcheck}
- [ ] The skill ran in a fresh session, on a real input, and I checked the output
:::

### 5. Stabilise

Once it works twice, make it something you can leave alone for a month:

- move anything you might tune (lengths, folders, formats, language) into a
  defaults block in `CLAUDE.md`;
- add a one-line note at the top saying what changed and when;
- try it on a second, different input;
- if a colleague should have it, give them the folder. That is the whole
  installation.

::: {#skill-step-5 .checklist .selfcheck}
- [ ] Defaults live in `CLAUDE.md`, and the skill has run on two different inputs
:::

## Patterns to steal from the sessions {#patterns}

Every one of these is in a session folder you can open and copy from.

| Pattern | What it buys you | Where to look |
|---|---|---|
| **Review gate** | Nothing final is written before you have seen the plan | The slide-plan confirmation in `/proposal-to-slides`; the structure prompt in `/report` |
| **Defaults in `CLAUDE.md`** | Change a page limit once, every skill follows | The defaults block at the top of each session's `CLAUDE.md` |
| **Intermediate files** | When the result is wrong, you can see which step to fix | `output/manifest.md` and `output/summaries/` in Session 2 |
| **Small skills plus an orchestrator** | Learn step by step, demo in one command | `/collect`, `/synthesize`, `/report` and `/summarizer` |
| **Stub plus readable recipe** | The command stays short; the procedure stays readable | `.claude/skills/collect/SKILL.md` pointing to `skills/collect.md` |
| **Optional argument with a default** | Works with no input, adapts when you give one | `/collect` versus `/collect path/to/folder` |
| **Separated roles** | The judge cannot be swayed by the gatherer | `/reviewer` reads only the briefing in Session 3 |
| **Cite or drop** | No claim without a source file and passage | The traceability rule in `/reviewer` |
| **Audit log** | A record of what was done, not what was said | `output/audit-log.md` in Session 3 |
| **Progress and summary blocks** | You can follow a long run without reading everything | The boxed headers and `✓` lines in every recipe |

## When a skill disappoints {#when-a-skill-disappoints}

Fix it straight away, in the folder where it went wrong, while the bad output
is still there to point at.

**Show the problem.**

```text
I just ran /my-task on input/q3-notes.md. I expected a one-page summary with
three decisions. I got four pages and no decisions. Read the skill and the
output, and tell me which instruction caused this. Do not change anything yet.
```

**Decide what to change.** There are two kinds of fault. A technical one (a
file was not found, a tool is missing) needs the environment fixed. An
instruction that is vague or out of date needs the skill reworded. Ask for the
smallest change that would have prevented this run.

**Have Claude make the change**, keeping the rest:

```text
Make the change we agreed on. Keep everything else in the skill as it is, and
add a dated one-line note at the top saying what changed and why.
```

**Re-run on the input that exposed the problem**, in a fresh session. If you
keep your folder in Git, the previous version of the skill is one command away
if the fix made things worse.

## Audit once in a while {#audit}

Skills accumulate. A few times a year, open the project and ask:

```text
List every skill in .claude/skills/ with one line on what it does. Which ones
overlap? Which refer to files or tools that no longer exist? Which have steps
you would not need today? Give me a short prioritised list. Change nothing.
```

Then work through the top of the list. Retiring a skill you no longer use is
progress too.

::: {.credit-note}
The lifecycle (notice, do by hand, write, test, stabilise) and the idea of a
"patterns to steal" table follow Chris Blattman's
[Create a skill](https://claudeblattman.com/build-your-own/building-skills/) and
[Fix and update your skills](https://claudeblattman.com/workflows/maintain-skills/).
The official reference is
[Skills in the Claude Code docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills).
:::
